speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The last comprehensive review of the Road Traffic Act, or RTA, was conducted more than five years ago, in 2019.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is timely that we do another review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) works closely with the Ministry of Transport (MOT) to keep our road users safe.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, regulations, such as the demerit points regime, to discourage risk-taking behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fourth, appropriate road infrastructure to ensure road safety, such as red-amber-green arrows restricting discretionary right turns, as well as Silver Zones and School Zones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Lastly, public education and engagement, including targeted initiatives for vulnerable road users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We regularly take stock of our efforts and make further improvements where necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Most recently, in 2024, we commenced the mandatory installation of speed limiters in lorries and activated the speed enforcement function in red-light cameras.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have also assessed that refinements are required in relation to certain offences and penalties in RTA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Members will recall that in 2019, we made comprehensive amendments to RTA, of which, three are relevant to today's Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, we enhanced the punishments for two classes of irresponsible driving offences, that is, dangerous driving and careless driving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Dangerous driving refers to driving a motor vehicle on a road recklessly or at a speed or in a manner which is dangerous to the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Careless driving is less serious than dangerous driving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It refers to driving on a road without due care and attention or without reasonable consideration for other persons using the road.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Dangerous or careless driving offences are punishable with a longer maximum imprisonment term and a higher maximum fine, than the corresponding Rash Act or Negligent Act offence in the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, we introduced a tiered approach for the penalties for these offences, based on the level of harm caused.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition to circumstances where there has been no hurt caused, the three levels of harm are death, grievous hurt and hurt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The more serious the harm, the more severe the penalties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Additional penalties apply for repeat offenders of certain driving offences and those who drive under the influence of drugs or alcohol, whom we refer to as "serious offenders".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, we introduced mandatory minimum sentences and minimum disqualification periods, for offences causing death and grievous hurt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For these offences, the law requires the Court to impose a minimum imprisonment term and minimum period of disqualification from driving, save for the exceptional circumstances, such as when responding to a medical emergency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The 2019 amendments sent a clear message: irresponsible driving will not be tolerated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We remain committed to deterring and punishing irresponsible driving behaviour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: That said, MHA has observed the impact of the 2019 amendments and identified areas where we should recalibrate the balance between deterrence and proportionality, particularly in cases where the circumstances of the offence indicate that the offending motorist might have a lower level of culpability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I will first speak about the amendments to recalibrate the balance between deterrence and proportionality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These are reflected in clause 5 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will give our Courts greater discretion to determine the appropriate sentence based on the circumstances, instead of the current situation where there are prescribed mandatory minimum sentences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To be clear, first-time offenders will still face penalties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These penalties will be determined based on factors including the nature and severity of the harm caused to the victim, and the level of culpability of the accused.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Members will be aware that the vast majority of criminal offences in our laws do not prescribe any minimum penalty.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Courts have discretion to impose a just sentence up to the statutory prescribed maximum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These amendments therefore bring the approach for first-time traffic offenders closer to the norm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A taxi driver, who is a first-time offender, beat a red turning arrow signal and collided into an oncoming motorcyclist who was speeding across the junction on an amber signal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As a result of the accident, the motorcyclist had pain, scratches and abrasions to the neck and shoulder, and received a total of 25 days of medical leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, it can be argued that the taxi driver is not as culpable because the motorcyclist had been speeding across the junction on an amber signal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The accident might not have occurred if the motorcyclist had slowed down and prepared to stop when the traffic light turned amber.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Government's view is that the Court should have the discretion to decide if a lesser sentence would be more proportionate to the culpability of the taxi driver and the extent of injuries suffered by the motorcyclist.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For the avoidance of doubt, these amendments do not necessarily mean that the offending motorist will face a sentence lower than the current mandatory minimum of one year imprisonment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Court, having full regard to the facts of the case, will ultimately decide the sentence, which may even be higher than the current statutory minimums.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The key point is, with the amendments, the Court will not be constrained by the statutory minimums.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This adjustment aims to create a more gradual progression in sentencing between first-time and repeat offenders under the new regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The intent of these amendments is not to signal a more lenient stance towards repeat offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Repeat offenders will continue to be subject to mandatory minimum imprisonment terms and disqualification periods, and where warranted on the circumstances, the Courts may in fact impose sentences higher than these mandatory minimum terms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I want to also emphasise that there is no change to the way we are treating serious offenders, especially those who drive irresponsibly while under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They will continue to receive severe penalties, as well as mandatory minimum penalties where grievous hurt or death is caused.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The driver failed to stop when ordered by a Traffic Police officer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the subsequent pursuit, the driver drove dangerously by filtering lanes rapidly and collided into a pedestrian crossing the road at a pedestrian crossing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The offending driver is charged with dangerous driving causing grievous hurt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: After the proposed amendments to the RTA are operationalised, there would be no mandatory minimum imprisonment sentence or disqualification period applicable to this offender.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, given the aggravating factors in this case, including the failure to heed a Traffic Police officer's instructions and engaging in more egregious behaviour that increased the risk of harm to the Traffic Police officer and other road users, the offender can expect to be sentenced to imprisonment and disqualified for periods that are longer than the mandatory minimums today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I emphasise that there are no changes to the maximum penalties for dangerous or careless driving offences, which could include lifetime imprisonment and lifetime disqualification from driving in highly egregious cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Sentencing Advisory Panel, chaired by Justice of the Court of Appeal Tay Yong Kwang, is looking at issuing guidelines for dangerous and careless driving offences, to enhance sentencing consistency and public understanding of the range of sentences that may be imposed under various scenarios.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, the Bill will provide the Prosecution flexibility to proceed on a "hurt" charge, even where "grievous hurt" has factually been caused.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Because of the manner in which the dangerous and careless driving offences are presently structured in the RTA, the High Court has ruled that where an injury designated as "grievous hurt" was factually caused as a result of the accused's driving, the Prosecution can only prefer a charge of dangerous or careless driving causing "grievous hurt" and not a charge of causing simple "hurt".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As a result of this ruling, if a driver drove carelessly and caused a pedestrian to sustain a fractured finger, the Prosecution presently does not have the discretion to proceed on a charge that is anything less severe than a "grievous hurt" charge.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Government's intent has always been to allow the Prosecution to exercise its discretion to prefer the appropriate charge – be it a "hurt" or "grievous hurt" charge – after taking into account the circumstances of each case.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This amendment restores the policy intent, and in my example, allows the Prosecution the discretion to proceed on a simple hurt charge if it assesses that it is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It also promotes consistency with our other penal provisions, by clarifying that "hurt" has the same meaning in the context of both the RTA and the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will also align the position for road traffic accidents with the Penal Code, where the Prosecution has the discretion to proceed on a "hurt" charge even if the assailant had, in fact, caused "grievous hurt".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, the Bill will adjust how a motorist's track record will count towards being classified as a repeat offender for a dangerous or careless driving offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Being classified as a repeat offender leads to enhanced penalties for the offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, a motorist is classified as a repeat offender if he has a prior conviction of dangerous driving, careless driving, speeding or illegal speed trial offence, colloquially known as illegal street racing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The threshold of 40 km/h in excess of the relevant speed limit is not new.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, most speeding offences are minor in nature and typically resolved with composition sums.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For the avoidance of doubt, any relevant antecedents from more than five years ago can still be taken into account by the Court as an aggravating factor when deciding on the sentence, but it will not attract the enhanced penalties that the RTA provides for those classified as repeat offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is no change to how prior convictions of other offences, such as dangerous and careless driving, will count towards a motorist's classification as a repeat offender.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 3, 11 and 14 of the Bill streamline the commencement date of the disqualification period for both the RTA and the Motor Vehicles (Third-Party Risks and Compensation) Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, for some offences, the commencement date of the disqualification period starts from the date of conviction, whereas for others, it starts from the date of release from prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In yet other cases, it may not be specified in the law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If the offender has an existing disqualification order and is imprisoned for any offence, the disqualification order will be suspended during the term of imprisonment and will resume immediately after the date of release from the sentence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If the offender does not receive an imprisonment term, the disqualification period will commence from the date of conviction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will ensure consistency and parity across the various disqualification regimes and remove irresponsible drivers from the roads in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 4 will also enhance the Traffic Police's immediate suspension powers by ensuring that a motorist's licence remains suspended until he is fully convicted or acquitted, including during the period of appeal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, the Traffic Police can immediately suspend the driving licence of any motorist under specific circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This includes where there was serious injury or death to a person or serious damage to buildings and structures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, the suspension automatically lapses by law once the motorist is convicted or acquitted by the Court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This means that if the motorist appeals, he can resume driving pending the determination of his appeal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As the suspension automatically lapses upon conviction, and he has been convicted, his suspension lapses by law, even though his appeal is pending.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The same can happen if the disqualification order against the motorist is deferred by the Court to start at a later date.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To be clear, if a motorist has been acquitted by the Court, regardless whether the Prosecution appeals against the acquittal, the suspension order will no longer be in force.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will enable the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) to more holistically discharge their protective security functions at the land and sea checkpoints, which they have taken over from the Police.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 10 will amend the RTA to incentivise owners to collect their seized vehicles in a timely manner and streamline the subsequent disposal process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The RTA currently only allows the Traffic Police to dispose of any vehicle within one month of its detention, if no owner comes forward to claim it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, there are vehicles that cannot be disposed of, as the vehicle owners have laid claim to them but have delayed collecting them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To address this issue, the Bill will require a vehicle owner to take delivery of a seized vehicle within a specified period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Traffic Police can recover storage costs from the owner if the owner fails to collect the seized vehicle within the collection period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Traffic Police will be able to dispose of the seized vehicle one month from after the expiry of the collection period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There are also several miscellaneous amendments to improve the Traffic Police's operational efficiency, such as clause 12, which amends section 131A of the RTA to allow summonses which are not punishable with imprisonment to be served by email.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The summons may only be served by email if the person on whom the summons is to be served gives prior written consent and specifies in the written consent the person's email address to which the summons is to be sent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Lastly, clause 15 repeals the School Crossing Patrols Act 1955.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Act is obsolete and the policy intent to ensure safe school crossings has been met by other means.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They are necessary to make our laws fairer while ensuring that those who engage in egregious road behaviour continue to be punished severely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, dangerous driving has no place on our roads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not just a rule of law.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a matter of life and death.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a good step forward, but it raises some questions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When this Bill was announced, Yio Chu Kang residents have asked me, "Are we sending the wrong message?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could undermine public trust and undo years of effort to foster safer driving habits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents are also concerned about consistency and fairness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that sentencing decisions are equitable and reflect the severity of offences?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will our Courts be guided on the minimum sentences for offences, now that it is removed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are real risks that we cannot ignore and may be exploited by offenders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Ministry must monitor the impact of these changes to ensure they do not compromise public safety.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Stronger penalties should go hand in hand with public campaigns to hammer home the message – reckless driving destroys lives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us make it clear that dangerous driving will not be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear communication about the gravity of penalties is essential to maintain public trust in our justice system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mdm Deputy Speaker, empowering immigration officers to conduct breath tests at checkpoints is a logical and necessary move.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Drunk driving is a menace that knows no borders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But as with any enforcement, the devil is in the details.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will officers be trained to exercise their powers impartially?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents have expressed concerns about potential profiling, which could erode public trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear guidelines and robust training must be non-negotiable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another worry is the perennial issue of delays at checkpoints, especially since our Woodlands Checkpoint is one of the busiest land crossing points in the world.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many people commute across these borders daily for work or family obligations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry leverage technology to speed up the process while ensuring strong enforcement?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The goal must always be to achieve safety without undue inconvenience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, how does the Ministry plan to deal with foreign vehicles that may have been caught committing traffic offences, especially speeding, illegal parking or beating the red light?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the ICA plan to enforce these fines and ensure that they are paid?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Across the border, our neighbours have already used various methods to ensure that Singaporean drivers pay up their fines.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are we doing something similar considering that our roads also have a number of foreign vehicles plying them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do we similarly enforce our laws on these foreign vehicles?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mdm Deputy Speaker, digitalising summons delivery may be a step into the future, but we must ensure no one is left behind in this transition.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Not every resident has email or the digital literacy to navigate online systems.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors, in particular, are at risk of being excluded.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Using email for those ready and physical mail for others ensures fairness during the shift to a digital process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This dual system approach would be a practical way to cater to the diverse needs of our population.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fraudulent summonses could trick people into revealing sensitive information or paying bogus fines.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need robust safeguards to protect against this.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Equally important is clear communication with the public about how to identify legitimate summonses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Each is essential to creating a safer and fairer road traffic system for all.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On dangerous driving, we must ensure penalties serve as a real deterrent while giving the Courts the discretion to impose sentences that match the severity of the harm caused.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This flexibility recognises that driving is a complex task requiring skill, focus and experience, and that mistakes can happen even to the best of us.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By striking this balance, we strengthen the rule of law while upholding fairness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On enforcement, empowering officers at checkpoints to combat drink driving is a necessary move.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it must be implemented with care, ensuring fairness, impartiality and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear guidelines and robust training are non-negotiable to maintain public trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Leveraging technology can help minimise inconvenience for commuters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On modernisation, transitioning to digital summons delivery is a step forward, but we must ensure inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors and the digitally disadvantaged must not be left behind and cybersecurity measures must be in place to protect residents from scams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A hybrid approach during this transition is not just practical, it is essential to maintaining public confidence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, this Bill is more than a collection of amendments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a commitment to protecting lives and livelihoods, especially those most vulnerable – our elderly, our low-wage workers – and those who depend on the road for their daily bread.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Behind every traffic law is a family waiting for their loved ones to return home safely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Behind every enforcement action is a promise to uphold justice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And behind every decision we make here is the opportunity to build a road system that does not just move people but safeguards lives.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) has some concerns with the proposed amendments to the Road Traffic Act that we hope the Government can address today.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's justification for making these amendments is that the current mandated minimums are too harsh and may cause some drivers to be overly punished as a result.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it is important to note that section 64 on reckless and dangerous driving already carries a higher level of culpability than driving without due care and attention in section 65.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Drivers who run red lights or drive recklessly at dangerous speeds are knowingly and wilfully putting other road users at risk.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In justifying the amendment, MHA have shared several examples where the current laws as applied would be too harsh.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two can be found in Annex A from MHA's press release on the Bill published on 11 November 2024.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another can be found in MHA's response on 29 November 2024 to letters from the public on The Straits Times Forum.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As it is currently not clear if these cases are purely hypothetical or based on actual cases, can the Minister clarify whether these examples are based on actual cases?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, none of these cases mentioned involved fatalities as a result of dangerous or careless driving.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister be able to share with this House some recent cases of dangerous driving leading to death where they believe the mandated minimum jail term of two years was too harsh?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans are baffled by the timing of this decision to do away with mandatory minimum penalties.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Online and offline, many members of the public have shared that the proposed changes would make the roads feel less safe for themselves, especially pedestrians and cyclists, and are concerned that the change would lead to a rise in the number of dangerous driving cases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These concerns are understandable given that there has been an increasing trend in the number of fatal accidents in recent years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The mandatory minimum sentences for dangerous driving causing death or grievous hurt had been introduced in 2019 in order to increase the sentencing norms for irresponsible driving offences and to avoid manifestly inadequate jail sentences for egregious offences.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Second Reading debate, then Second Minister for Home Affairs, Mrs Josephine Teo, said that irresponsible driving remained a big concern.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if victims survive the accident, they or their families may suffer long-term problems – sometimes, medical, sometimes, permanent disabilities." From time to time, we hear of terrible tragedies on the road.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, on 22 April, a driver sped and ran a red light in Tampines.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Six vehicles were involved in the accident and two people died.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Afifah Munirah Muhammad Azril was a 17-year-old student at Temasek Junior College who was described as a high flier in school.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their lives came to a tragic end because of irresponsible driving.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Strong deterrence is needed against irresponsible driving behaviours leading to death, which is irreversible.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2019, Mrs Teo said, "motorists who have a blatant disregard for the safety of other road users should be severely punished" and "to make our roads safer, we need stronger deterrence against irresponsible driving".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, why is there an apparent policy U-turn by the Government today with the removal of mandatory minimum jail terms for first-time offenders even in cases of reckless or dangerous driving leading to death?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on figures from the Singapore Police Force (SPF), the number of fatal accidents dropped in 2020 when compared to 2019, but thereafter increased every year from 2021 to 2023.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, we debated the issue of dangerous driving in this House after the six-vehicle crash in Tampines on 22 April 2024 where a driver sped, ran a red light and caused the tragic deaths of two persons.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the time, the Government rejected calls to consider introducing stiffer penalties for road traffic offences.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, we hear that the Government is, in fact, going to do the opposite, by removing the mandatory minimum penalties for first-time offenders.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we work towards a car-lite society, where the privilege of owning and driving a car is for the minority, we must consider the interests of road users who are not motorists.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By retaining mandatory minimum jail terms, we send a clear message to motorists that they have the responsibility for helping to keep other road users safe and there would be serious consequences should they wilfully fail to do so.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to Police data, there has been a significant increase of fatal traffic accidents from 2020 to 2023.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many citizens are, therefore deeply concerned about road safety.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2019, the Government implemented mandatory minimum sentences for reckless driving behaviour.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then Second Minister for Home Affairs Josephine Teo said that drivers who blatantly disregard the safety of other road users should be severely punished.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendment) Bill today proposes to amend the Road Traffic Act 1961 and the Motor Vehicles (Third Party Risks and Compensation) Act 1960 and to repeal the School Crossing Patrol Act of 1955.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In justifying the reason for the amendments, MHA has, in its advisory in November 2024, explained that today's amendments were part of their regular review, the last being done in 2019.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are told that the amendment is required as there is a need to adjust the Act to balance deterrence and proportionality, which applicable sentencing principles which the Court will abide by.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Importantly, MHA has explained that the changes will ensure that behaviour that is relatively less egregious is not overly penalised, while the law can still be used to penalise egregious offenders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, the Court will be able to give lighter sentences where other road users have also behaved irresponsibly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On one hand, there are Singaporeans who are concerned that the removal of the minimum sentences will represent a relaxation of the laws on careless or reckless driving.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such concerns are understandable, especially bearing in mind recent high-profile serious road traffic accidents, such as the road accident at the junction of Tampines Avenue 1 and Tampines Avenue 4 in April 2024, where a driver failed to stop at the traffic junction and caused an accident involving five other vehicles and leading to the unfortunate death of two persons.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It was also reported, more recently on 18 December 2024 that a driver was sentenced to a year's imprisonment and disqualified from driving for eight years after he pleaded guilty to three charges of causing death of a pedestrian in October 2022 by driving without due care and attention, failing to render assistance and obstructing the course of justice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The driver was previously fined $500 and handed 12 demerit points for speeding just a month before the fatal accident.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The victim was a 26-year-old pharmacist and who was a Hougang resident of mine.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In fact, in light of similar serious traffic accidents in recent years, some Singaporeans have asked whether we should enhance our laws to deter reckless driving and serious road accidents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Following the accident at Tampines Avenue 1, I and some other Members of this House have asked questions, and the Government addressed some of such concerns in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I trust that the Government will assure Singaporeans today that the proposed changes in this Bill will not lead to a relaxation of the law or the enforcement efforts against careless or reckless driving and result in a worsening of the present situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under this Bill, the prosecution will be able to proceed with a charge of causing hurt and are not grievous hurt if the victim's injuries meet the legal definition of grievous hurt.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Grievous hurt is defined under section 320 of the Penal Code and it can include fractures or dislocations and when the victim cannot follow his or her ordinary pursuits for at least 20 days.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: MHA explained that the change under this Bill will better allow the Prosecution to take into account the nature of the injury caused and whether other road users share responsibility for the incident.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The definition of repeat offender will also be narrowed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, a motorist is a repeat offender if he or she has been convicted previously of any one of the following: dangerous or careless driving, conducting illegal speed trials or speeding.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I ask this as some Singaporeans will regard speeding in excess of lower speed ranges, such as between 20 and 39 km/h, or 30 and 39 km/h, to be already excessive and deserving of the current minimum punishment under the present law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore still suffers from a significant number of deaths and injuries from road traffic accidents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Road traffic accidents in 2023 also caused 8,931people to suffer non-fatal injuries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: According to the Annual Road Traffic Situation Report 2023, road traffic fatalities have increased year-on-year since 2020, from a low of 83 during COVID to 136 in 2023.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The current number of annual fatalities are also higher than the pre-COVID numbers: 136 in 2023 versus 118 in 2019.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Similarly, the traffic accident cases involving injuries have similarly increased year on year since 2020, from 6,669 in 2020 to 8,931 in 2023.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: MHA also mentioned two past cases justifying the Government's intention to remove minimum sentences.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Two examples: the first case involves a taxi driver who fails to conform to a red-light signal at a T-junction and collides into an oncoming motorcar, which has the right of way.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The victim sustained neck and shoulder pain with numbness in one half of his body and received a medical certificate (MC) for 25 days.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But a subsequent medical assessment finds that the victim has made a full recovery.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Because the victim has received at least 20 days of MC and section 320 of the Penal Code defines grievous hurt as, among other things, any hurt that causes the victim to be unable to follow his or her ordinary pursuits during the space of 20 days.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This meant that the injury to the victim in the cited case was regarded as grievous hurt under the law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is notwithstanding that the overall injury sustained, suffered, was not actually that severe, having regard to the initial injury report and the victim's full recovery.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, the driver in the first example may be regarded as objectively reckless in running the red light and it may be argued that whether the victim is more or less injured is just a matter of fortuity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Another criticism is that the problem may not be the minimum sentence itself, but the definition of grievous hurt under section 320 of the Penal Code, especially as we now see how it has applied to the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, the factual scenario seen in the first example cited by MHA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Further, there is also the issue of whether the length of an MC necessarily commensurate with the seriousness of the injury caused and has a definitive bearing on, say, permanent incapacity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A more restricted discretion may result in drivers being penalised unnecessarily or unnecessarily harsh.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In some cases, the punishment may have more serious consequences or resulting in loss of jobs and/or deprivation of employment income and resulting financial hardship.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is, however, important for the Courts to create clear guidelines after the law is amended so that drivers are punished more appropriately according to what they have done and are not overly punished.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am, therefore, heartened to hear the Minister of State sharing just now to the House that this will be carried out by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also agree with MHA's explanation in their second example where a driver collided with a cyclist who failed to give way to the driver and cross the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am of the view that in accidents where both a driver and the other road user, could be a motorist, failed to give way to each other or were both guilty of different traffic offences, resulting in a collision.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: MHA should not over penalise one party merely because another party was physically injured.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Using the second case example given by MHA, the primary consideration upon which punishment should be imposed should first be the primary wrongfulness, if any, of both parties leading to the accident, rather than merely of the cyclist being injured.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In MHA's example, there is the failure of the cyclist to stop and give way and there is also the failure of the driver to keep a proper lookout for a cyclist in breach of the cyclist's own legal obligations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There should be greater and appropriate proportionality given to both road users for their respective breaches.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If they are more seriously taken to task when they are found to be in breach, this may encourage a change in our riding culture on the roads and enhance the safety of our roads and accidents can be minimised or prevented.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Further, it is also not uncommon for parties involved in accidents to latch on to the Traffic Police's charges against particular motorists to argue that their opponent's case may be weaker.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If successful, this, together with the law of contributory negligence, may mean that in the ensuing civil claims, a motorist may be the ultimate paying party in such a case where another road user who also blatantly breaks the law is injured.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The accident involved a side swipe with a motorcyclist, resulting in the latter suffering a fracture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Another resident said that with the change, there may be the anomaly arising from those who were more recently punished under the RTA 2019 coming out from their disqualification period even later than those who may be sentenced under the RTA 2024, assuming that this will be passed in the near future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given the change in law and the rationale given by MHA for the change, there may be an issue of fairness.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As such, will the Government address the above concerns?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The argument is that such offences should be distinguished from other crimes if such offences arose purely as an accident, that there was no deliberate intent to break the law or to commit the offence, and there was no premeditation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There may be consequences or burdens on the convicted in terms of employment or travel when declarations for such convictions are required.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This proposal reflects a positive shift from current practice and demonstrates a more sophisticated approach to justice and sentencing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Context matters and judges should always have discretion in sentencing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Defendants before a Court should always be allowed to present and have considered mitigating circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Roads are public and shared spaces where mistakes can have devastating consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We all know of someone who has been impacted by the behaviour of other drivers or even ourselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is understandable that the community want to see justice done if and when a crime occurs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am not saying that court processes, including sentencing, should be determined by community outrage or preference, but the views of the community need to be acknowledged and considered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps it would be appropriate for these proposed amendments to be accompanied by a public awareness campaign, reinforcing the message that the removal of mandatory sentences for first-time traffic offenders is not going soft on crime or letting people get away with things, but is instead an evidence-based sentencing practice that leads to greater desistance and reduced recidivism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to inform the public that the primary aim of these changes is to make our roads safer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: MHA has highlighted that they would monitor and report on sentencing patterns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, it would be good if it could look at the trends over time and look at the trends because courts as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Alternatively, perhaps the Ministry could consider establishing dedicated traffic courts, presided over by specialist magistrates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This would assist to ensure that the sentencing of traffic offenders is nationally appropriate and consistent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Ministry could commit to an evaluation of the impact of the proposed changes after, for example, one, three or five years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Traffic accidents are already the top killer of children and young people aged between five and 29 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Our roads should be safe for everyone and just like Singapore has zero tolerance for drug use, we should also have zero tolerance for injury and fatality caused by traffic or road accidents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Some accidents are simply mistakes – a momentary lapse of reason and judgement by an otherwise responsible driver.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Others are a lack of awareness about traffic and driving safety or an over confidence or lack of awareness about personal skill and competence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Far too many others are the result of predominantly young men showing off in front of their friends, thinking that reckless driving or behaviour is cool or exciting or that they are invincible to such harms on the road.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Some are the result of deliberate, repeated and purposeful behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: According to deterrence theory, individuals make behavioural choices based on their perceptions of the threat posed by penalties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This perceived threat is influenced by the likelihood of being caught, or perceived risk of apprehension and beliefs about the certainty, severity and swiftness of punishments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A penalty-based system can be very effective in many cases, however, not all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Fining, imposing disqualification periods or even imprisonment can have little short- or long-term effect on an alarming number of road users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also need comprehensive education programmes that provide drivers and other road users with age, gender and culturally appropriate information and messaging about road and traffic safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These programmes also need to target different categories of road users, including motorcyclists, motorcycle passengers, peddle or electric cyclists, companies transporting foreign workers, children and young people, and elderly pedestrians.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Ideally, we need to convince people to stop wanting to do or choosing to do the many things on the road that can get themselves or someone else killed or seriously injured.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In these circumstances, instead of – or sometimes as well as – a fine or other punitive consequences, convicted drivers are referred to alternatives aimed at changing future behaviour, including driving courses, awareness programmes, rehabilitation support or community service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: When the concept of Vision Zero was introduced in 1997, it transformed the view of road safety work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of trying to prevent all accidents, the goal is for no one to die or be seriously injured in a road accident.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Vision Zero regards the road transport system as an entity in which different components such as roads, vehicles and road users must be made to interact with each other so that safety can be guaranteed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To prevent serious consequences from accidents, it is essential for roads and vehicles to be adapted to match the capabilities of the people who use them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This topic has been discussed a number of times in Parliament and advocacy groups have been calling for a ban on unsecured open vehicle transport for several years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It involves fostering a culture of responsible driving and road use and ensuring that our justice system balances accountability with rehabilitation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Our goal should be not just to punish offenders but to prevent accidents, support victims and enhance safety for all road users in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we can create a safer environment for everyone who calls Singapore home.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also strongly support the provision of enhanced powers to our Traffic Police to enforce our regulations against errant motorists.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is understandable that the authorities want to adjust penalties to be more proportionate to particular offences.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This reduction is too lenient, even for first-time offenders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to remember that in these cases, lives had been, or could have been endangered, or lost, and the offenders did exhibit dangerous or careless driving behaviour in causing the accidents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The penalties need to be severe enough to act effectively as a meaningful deterrence.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As it is today, as many drivers observe on our roads, there are quite a number of motorists speeding, tailgating or driving carelessly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We cannot afford to reduce the penalties further to send the wrong message to such motorists.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Why do we need a motorist to have committed such offences at least twice, while continuing to drive irresponsibly, before we consider him or her a repeat offender?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is not the behaviour of an average motorist at all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am concerned that most will perceive that the Ministry is becoming lenient on such offenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They raised important questions which I will now attempt to address.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Members raised concerns over the removal of mandatory minimums.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked for the reason for the proposed amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As explained in my earlier speech, MHA reviews the offences and penalties in the RTA from time to time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As pointed out by Ms Poa, we have provided some examples to illustrate the need for these amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how the Ministry will ensure that sentences are equitable and reflect the severity of offences, and how our Courts will be guided on the minimum sentences for offences, given the removal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Assoc Prof Razwana suggested establishing dedicated Traffic Courts to ensure sentences are consistent and appropriate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Regarding Mr Yip's concern, it is precisely because of the need for fairness that we are moving these amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Our intent is indeed to ensure that the RTA penalties reflect the severity of the offence, as well as the culpability of the offender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Sentencing decisions are made by the Courts, which will consider the facts and circumstances of every case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Regarding Assoc Prof Razwana's suggestion of dedicated Traffic Courts, it is already the case today, in practice that if the motorist faces only traffic charges, his case will generally be heard in the Traffic Court.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To enhance sentencing consistency and transparency, the Sentencing Advisory Panel is also looking at issuing guidelines for dangerous and careless driving offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This will provide guidance to the Judges on the sentencing approach for such offences, while allowing them to decide the exact sentence for each case depending on its own facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip asked if lighter sentences could embolden risky behaviour and lead to more repeat offenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Assoc Prof Razwana, Mr Dennis Tan and Ms Hazel Poa were also concerned that the amendments would send the wrong message to offenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I wish to reiterate that the intent of these amendments is not to signal a more lenient stance towards egregious motorists, nor to let them off with lighter sentences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will continue to punish those who exhibit irresponsible driving behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The maximum penalties are stiff and remain unchanged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Judges will have full flexibility to decide the appropriate sentence up to the maximum sentence prescribed in law, depending on the facts of each case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked if there were any recent cases of dangerous driving causing death, for which we believe the mandatory minimum imprisonment of two years is too harsh.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There are no such cases because in the appropriate circumstances, the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) had exercised its prosecutorial discretion to prefer a lesser charge, for example, to proceed on a careless driving charge, even though there was dangerous driving involved, or a charge involving hurt, even though grievous hurt was caused.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, this is not a fully satisfactory approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Moreover, as mentioned in my opening speech, the High Court has recently ruled that the Prosecution presently does not have the discretion to prefer a hurt charge where grievous hurt is factually caused.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, it goes back to about balancing the discretion and also the proportionality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked about the rationale for only taking into consideration a prior conviction of speeding in excess of 40 km/h.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The existing practice is that any offender who has sped in excess of 40 km/h of the relevant limit will generally be prosecuted in Court.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is not new, and is part of the calibrated approach that MHA takes towards speeding offences, such that more egregious speeding is dealt with through prosecution, and less egregious speeding is generally dealt with through our demerit points and the composition regime.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The amendment simply formalises this approach in law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked for the rationale of having at least two counts of prior speeding convictions before the motorist is considered a repeat offender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The amendment we are introducing today is part of the recalibration of the balance between deterrence and proportionality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It ensures that less serious offences are not overly penalised, while still allowing the Courts to take egregious offenders to task.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Specifically, the RTA explicitly provides for heavier penalties, including mandatory minimum sentences, in the event that the motorist meets the legal definition of a repeat offender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Where the motorist is currently being charged for a dangerous or careless driving offence and is a repeat offender within the meaning in the Act, the Courts must, if it finds the motorist guilty, impose heavier penalties that are specified in the RTA, including a minimum mandatory disqualification period ranging from five to 10 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To be clear, a motorist with prior speeding convictions, but who does not satisfy the legal definition of a repeat offender, may not necessarily be sentenced as if he had a clean record.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In such a case, the Court can continue to take into account his prior speeding convictions, when deciding on the sentence for a current dangerous or careless driving offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In other words, such a motorist can continue to expect heavier penalties to be imposed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Tan asked if those who were previously sentenced to the mandatory disqualification under the existing law will be allowed to have their period of disqualification reduced accordingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Concluded cases would have been sentenced under the previous offence provisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: That being said, for cases where the offender committed their driving offences before this amendment, AGC will consider the facts and circumstances of these cases, and adjust their sentencing position where it is fair to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Tan asked about our plans to curb the increase in road traffic fatalities and injuries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked about existing efforts to shape motorists' behaviour, including education or rehabilitation programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We adopt a multi-pronged approach to keep our roads in Singapore safe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In addition to our reviewing laws and regulations, other key prongs include enforcement, education and engagement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In terms of enforcement, the Traffic Police deploys a suite of enforcement tools to detect and deter against road traffic violations, which includes fixed speed cameras, red-light cameras, as well as routine patrols by Traffic Police officers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The speed cameras are deployed at speeding-prone and accident-prone locations, where the terrain is suitable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For education and engagement, the Traffic Police raises awareness on good road safety habits through online and in-person events such as talks, exhibitions and carnivals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Traffic Police also worked with the Singapore Road Safety Council and other stakeholders to organise campaigns targeted at different groups of road users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These include the "Road Safety Carnival for Families", "Anti-Drink Drive Campaign" and "Singapore Ride Safe" event that is targeted at motorcyclists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: When there are egregious cases of reckless and dangerous road behaviour, the Traffic Police will issue media releases to educate the public on the facts, charges and sentences for these cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As for rehabilitation programmes, the Traffic Police has introduced the Safe Driving Course for motorists who have accumulated demerit points, but are not yet liable for suspension.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The course educates these motorists on safe driving practices and corrects their risky behaviours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Upon completion of the course, the motorist will have some of their demerit points expunged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Assoc Prof Razwana spoke about support for accident victims and the use of restorative justice procedures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Police may refer families who require support to Social Service Offices or Family Service Centres, depending on their circumstances and needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For those requiring mental health support, the Police may refer them to mental health helplines and counselling services, which are run by trained professionals or the Institute of Mental Health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While there are no specific restorative justice programmes for traffic offences, certain features of our sentencing regime, such as criminal compensation orders, are restorative in nature and seek to redress the harm to the victim.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Assoc Prof Razwana also suggested monitoring sentencing trends and the impact of the amendments on driving behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked for an update on the transport arrangements for foreign workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Ministry of Transport has given a comprehensive reply in July 2023 on this issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Given that these are not the focus of this Bill, we invite the Member to file a separate Parliamentary Question on this matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will now deal with questions pertaining to the enhancement of our enforcement powers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the training of immigration officers to exercise their powers and whether the Ministry could leverage technology to speed up the process and avoid potential delays at checkpoints.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Today, immigration officers already assess if there is any suspected drink-driving violation at the checkpoints.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The key difference is that today, the immigration officer has to activate a Police officer to conduct an alcohol breath test, as only a Police officer is legally empowered to conduct the test.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, there should be no impact on congestion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On the contrary, traffic flow may even be enhanced, since these tests can be conducted more quickly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Officers deployed at the frontline will undergo the appropriate training to administer the tests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Next, Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about our approach for foreign vehicles with outstanding fines for traffic and illegal parking offences, as well as the number of foreign vehicles caught for traffic violations in 2023.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Foreign motorists who enter Singapore must abide by Singapore's laws.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They should settle any outstanding fines for traffic, parking or vehicular emissions offences promptly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We take violations by foreign motorists just as seriously as we do violations by local motorists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The authorities also regularly conduct operations against foreign motorists who commit offences in Singapore and do not settle their fines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We also issue public advisories regularly to remind foreign motorists to check the AXS website for any outstanding fines and to settle them promptly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Members of the public who are unsure about the legitimacy of any communication from the Police can call the ScamShield hotline at 1799.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I call upon all road users – motorists, cyclists, pedestrians, Members of the House and others – to uphold a culture of vigilance and courtesy on our roads.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Why was judicial discretion not an issue in 2019 but is now an issue in 2025?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As I shared earlier, we review our law from time to time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I also want to assure the Member that even though we will remove the minimum element of it, the Court will look at the facts of the case and it will enable more flexibility and a fairer outcome in the judgment.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Are there any Members who wish to have their dissent recorded?

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Hazel Poa, you did mention earlier that you did not support the Bill.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: So, would you like for your dissent to be recorded?

speaker: The Chairman
text: The citation year "2024" will be changed to "2025", as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Would Members who wish for their dissent to be recorded, please stand?

speaker: The Chairman
text: If Members want to say no, you should say no.
